newsitem.title: UK: Russia's GUM sees '96 net rising to $50 million.
newsitem.headline: Russia's GUM sees '96 net rising to $50 million.

text.p: Russia's leading retailer, Trade House GUM expects 1996 net income to rise to $50 million from last year's $29.5 million, company adviser Vladimir Tiurin said.
He also told a conference in London that sales were likely to reach $250 million from $199 million in 1995.
GUM plans to spend $192 million on developing its main retail site in Moscow, of which $70 million will come from internal resources.
"The remainder will come from outside sources, loans and a commercial partner," said company vice president Anatoly Stepanov.
He said GUM was currently in talks with potential foreign partners with "retail experience".
The rebuilding programme for the main store, which accounts for 68 percent of sales, will start in 1997 and be complete by 2004.
The development will increase retail space to 27,500 square metres from 16,000 at present.
Tiurin said that the reconstruction would not disrupt GUM's sales as the company would make use of the basement and add another storey within the building on Red Square.
"Also we have a smaller building which we will move one fifth of our customers into," he said.
Seventy-eight percent of GUM's customers are under 40 years old and tend to come from Russia's upper middle class.
"We aim to serve people whose shopping alternative is overseas," Tiurin said.

The capital accounts for 95 percent of sales, but GUM is also expanding outside Moscow and plans that its five stores in the regions, Smolensk, Orel, Kostroma, Tambov and Magnitorsk, will break even within two years of opening.
Tiurin said that GUM, in which western investors already have a 40 percent stake, would appoint five foreigners to its 15 member board of directors.
Banque Paribas, which organised the Russia conference, rates the share a buy at $20, despite its bull run this year.
"We would argue that a prospective price earnings ratio of around three times makes this liquid stock attractive to investors," Paribas said.
